stages.name: Government intervention: monopoly and mergers
stages.title: Government intervention: monopoly and mergers
stages.sub: Why and how governments step in to limit monopoly power and control mergers.

steps.q: One firm supplies 90% of the bottled water in a country, with no close rivals. Can it raise its price without losing most of its customers?
steps.right: Yes, because buyers have nowhere else to go
steps.wrong: No, buyers would all switch to rivals
steps.hint: Think about how many alternatives buyers actually have.
steps.pre: Being able to set price above the competitive level like this shows the firm has

steps.q: This dominant firm sets a higher price and produces less than a competitive market would. What has it gained control over?
steps.right: The price and output in the market
steps.wrong: Only the wages it pays its workers
steps.hint: What exactly can this firm decide that a small competitive firm cannot?

steps.q: Because of this power, the firm charges more and produces less than the socially ideal amount, while making large profits from consumers who have no choice. Would a government want to leave this alone?
steps.right: No, it would want to intervene
steps.wrong: Yes, it would leave the market as it is
steps.hint: Think about consumers paying more and getting less than what is efficient.

steps.wrong: A combination of a supplier and its customer

steps.q: A supermarket chain merges with its main rival, who sells the very same products in the same towns at the same stage of the supply chain. What type of merger is this, compared with buying an unrelated firm?
steps.wrong: A merger with an unrelated business
steps.hint: Are the two firms rivals selling the same thing, or completely unrelated businesses?

steps.q: Instead, that same supermarket buys up its milk supplier, a firm further back in its own supply chain. Is this a merger with a rival, or with a firm at a different stage of the same chain?
steps.right: A firm at a different stage of the same supply chain
steps.wrong: A direct rival selling the same product
steps.hint: The supplier does not compete with the supermarket for the same customers.
steps.pre: A merger with a firm at a different stage of the same supply chain is a

steps.q: Now the supermarket instead buys an unrelated clothing retailer, in a completely different market. Does this firm compete with the supermarket, or supply it?
steps.right: Neither, it is in an unrelated market
steps.wrong: It competes directly with the supermarket
steps.hint: Clothing retail and grocery are separate markets with no supply link.

steps.q: A government wants to check proposed mergers before they go ahead and reduce competition. Would it need a body that investigates deals before they are finalised?
steps.wrong: No, the firms can decide this themselves
steps.hint: Someone has to assess the risk to competition before the deal completes.

steps.q: After investigating, this body can approve a merger, approve it with conditions attached, or stop it going ahead entirely, using set thresholds. What do the thresholds, the investigation and the possible outcomes make up together?
steps.right: A set framework guiding every decision
steps.wrong: A one-off decision for each merger
steps.hint: Think about the overall set of rules and decisions used to manage mergers, not one single decision.
